duet.problem: Discrete graph navigation from language, RGB panoramas and simulator-provided pose/neighbour connectivity; REVERIE/SOON also require final object grounding. The full graph is hidden at inference, but each observation provides navigable neighbours and coordinates. This is a materially privileged sensing/action interface compared with monocular continuous robot control (§3, p 3).
duet.method:
AUTHOR METHOD: encode panorama views/objects, average them for visited-node features, and accumulate partial views for unseen frontier nodes. A growing graph records visited and navigable locations. The 768-D text encoder feeds a coarse graph transformer and a fine local cross-modal transformer. Graph attention adds a learned scalar transform of pairwise path distance to QKᵀ/√d (Eqs 3–4); this biases topology without a hard connectivity attention mask. Local neighbour logits are mapped to global actions, pooling visited-neighbour scores into a backtrack score (Eq 6). A sigmoid gate combines coarse/fine logits (Eqs 7–8). Visited nodes are normally masked as selected exploration destinations, yet shortest routes to frontier goals may traverse them.

TRAINING: MLM, masked-region classification, single-action prediction and object grounding where available initialize the transformer. Cross-entropy behavioural cloning is supplemented by pseudo-interactive demonstrations from full training graphs (Eqs 9–12), reducing exposure mismatch. The expert selects useful graph destinations; released R2R code also supports an nDTW expert and teacher-forced sequence targets. REVERIE setup uses 100k pretraining iterations, batch 32, two P100s; 20k finetuning iterations, batch 8, one P100 (§4.3 p 6). INFERENCE: grow map, score actions, route through known graph with Floyd shortest paths, cache stop scores and choose final location. Quadratic graph attention/path-distance storage grows with explored nodes; no fixed-memory guarantee is established.

Extended appendix A.1, PDF pp 11–12, supplies the pretraining targets: masked language modeling masks 15% of tokens and minimizes −log p(w_i | W_without_i, trajectory), with a vocabulary classifier on the averaged coarse/fine text features. Masked region classification zeros 15% of final-view features and minimizes KL(P_teacher || P_model) over ImageNet view or Visual Genome object classes. These soft labels supervise semantic reconstruction, not correctness of instruction completion. Appendix B, p 13, gives R2R pretraining 200k steps, batch 64, then 20k fine-tuning steps, batch 8, selecting by validation-unseen SPL; dataset-specific schedules differ.
duet.novelty: Relative to HAMT, adds global frontier selection and explicit topological relations; relative to prior graph navigators, combines graph-aware transformer reasoning with fine local object grounding. Table 1 isolates local/coarse/fused policies, Table 2 graph awareness, Table 3 training losses; a full leaderboard gain alone does not isolate architecture.
duet.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: R2R Table 7 p 8 gives DUET 72 SR/60 SPL on val-unseen and 69/59 test-unseen, versus HAMT-e2e 66/61 and 65/60. Higher SR therefore does not imply more efficient successful paths. REVERIE Table 6 gives val-unseen 46.98 SR, 33.73 SPL, 32.15 RGS. Table 4 p 7 finds synthetic instructions help pretraining but adding them during PID finetuning does not improve this configuration. Verdict: strong explicit exploration and grounding architecture, with an acknowledged backtracking/length tradeoff. OSR–SR measures endpoint selection loss conditional on visited trajectory; it does not identify softmax competition as the unique or primary cause.

Extended appendix C.2–C.4, PDF pp 13–14, explicitly reports backtracking in 48.6% of REVERIE unseen trajectories and 23.2% of R2R unseen trajectories, directly contradicting a no-return interpretation of visited-node masking. REVERIE unseen outcomes are 29.82% wrong room, 23.20% correct room but wrong location, and 46.98% correct location; object grounding conditional on the correct location is 68.43%. These are dataset-specific descriptive categories, not evidence that one softmax denominator causes all stopping failures. Figure 8 shows different outcomes for paraphrases describing the same path. Appendix Table 9 also shows a tradeoff between SR and grounding-weighted SPL as behavioral-cloning weight changes, rather than a uniformly optimal loss weight.
duet.implementation:
INSPECTED CODE: global visited-node masks coexist with shortest-path backtracking. A material paper/code distinction is that the paper specifically describes final return on forced timeout, while this pinned R2R rollout applies maximum cached stop-probability return whenever an episode ends. Sampled training forces stopping at the exact ground-truth endpoint, whereas testing uses predicted stop. These are diagnosis candidates, not demonstrated bugs or demonstrated performance causes. Reproduction needs licensed MP3D assets, precomputed features and checkpoints; imports include legacy NumPy aliases, so current Python compatibility is not established.

scalevln.problem: Insufficient environment diversity and trajectory-language supervision for generalization. ScaleVLN constructs training data; DUET+ScaleVLN is a trained DUET configuration, not a new independent architecture. Uses HM3D/Gibson simulator meshes, navigability oracles, rendered RGB and an existing instruction speaker.
scalevln.method: AUTHOR METHOD (§3 pp 3–4): sample navigable positions at minimum 0.4m separation, agglomeratively cluster at 1m, initially connect nearby points≤5m with degree cap 5, refine connectivity/traversability, render panoramas, repair mesh artifacts using a Co-Mod GAN trained on rendered/camera pairs, enumerate shortest paths with 3–5 intermediate nodes, then use EnvDrop speaker. Result 4,941,710 pairs from 800 HM3D plus 491 Gibson scenes. Training: CLIP-B/16 features; DUET for R2R/CVDN/REVERIE and HAMT plus waypoint predictor for R2R-CE. MLM/SAP pretraining is favored over also using MRM; DAgger finetuning mixes human and selected augmented data. R2R reported 20k pretraining iterations, batch 256, learning rate 5e-5, about 72 GPU-hours; finetuning peak about 48 GPU-hours (§4.1 p 5). Inference is the original navigator; no online generator required.
scalevln.novelty: Data construction quality and a component-level study of graph quality, environment count, image restoration, instruction generator and train-stage mixing. Tables 1–7 isolate these choices more usefully than the strongest leaderboard variant, which changes visual backbone and adds EnvEdit.
scalevln.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 9 p 8 distinguishes base DUET+ScaleVLN test 77 SR/68 SPL from starred EnvEdit+CLIP-H/14 variant 80/70; original DUET 69/59. Table 2 p 6 holds 700k samples while varying scenes; unseen SPL rises 64.59→65.32→66.00 for 200→400→800 scenes. Table 5 compares EnvDrop SR 76.59/SPL 67.74 against GPT-2 SR 75.82/SPL 66.08. Table 7 shows MLM+SAP 76.59 SR/67.74 SPL versus adding MRM 75.82/66.62. Verdict: compelling evidence for data/scene quality, without establishing a universal scaling law or language independence. Its suggestion to investigate stopping comes from remaining OSR–SR, not a causal stop-mechanism intervention.

Supplement Table 5 shows improved R4R route fidelity: nDTW 51.21→52.77 and SDTW 30.00→32.73 after scaling, alongside SR 43.97→45.60. This is counterevidence to a blanket claim that scaling necessarily weakens instruction following. Supplement Table 4 lists Seq2Seq SR 37.34→47.51, a 10.17 percentage-point difference; nearby prose says 12.2 points, an arithmetic inconsistency. REVERIE supplementary Table 6 shows higher navigation SR does not guarantee higher grounding: validation RGS 35.76 is below AutoVLN 36.58. These comparisons do not causally measure language reliance.

srdf.title: Bootstrapping Language-Guided Navigation Learning with Self-Refining Data Flywheel
srdf.versions: The second supplied file has the exact same SHA256 as the main PDF and adds no independent evidence. Main includes appendices; Algorithm 1 and extra scorer/generator experiments on pp 20–21 were inspected.
srdf.problem: Generate abundant aligned path-language supervision without new human annotation in the iterative loop. Assumes an initial human seed set, unlabeled simulator trajectories, pretrained multimodal generator and a trainable navigator. It is not training-free or free of human-created supervision.
srdf.method:
AUTHOR METHOD (§3 pp 4–6): LoRA-finetune Mantis-8B-SigLIP with interleaved image/action trajectory prompts. Greedy captions form candidate generator-training data; top-k sampled diverse captions train DUET. Train/fine-tune navigator, rerun generated instructions, retain generator candidates satisfying SPL=1 and navigator samples with nDTW≥0.9. Regenerate failed samples rather than changing the trajectory pool; repeat 3 rounds, plus fourth generator refinement. Dataset 20,417,874 instructions across 860 environments. InternViT-6B encodes images except CLIP-B/16 in CE; navigator 45k iterations, batch 1024, learning rate 5e-5, 8 A100s, then R2R 6k iterations batch 16 (§4.1 p 7). At inference only trained navigator is used. No theorem establishes monotonic improvement or verifier correctness.

Appendix A.1, PDF p 19, clarifies that RxR-English and R4R use recovery to a reference-path viewpoint maximizing nDTW rather than a universal shortest-path expert. R2R and other tasks use shortest-path teacher actions. This distinction is essential when evaluating whether the flywheel preserves route semantics. Generator training updates LoRA layers on Mantis-8B-SigLIP-Llama 3; the round 3 navigator and generator reuse round 2 initialization while earlier rounds restart specified base models.
srdf.novelty: Relative to Speaker-Follower/ScaleVLN, jointly improves generator and navigator through navigation-consistency filtering and targeted recaptioning. Unlike mere scaling, quality changes at fixed underlying trajectory pool; Table 3 tracks rounds, Tables 4/11 compare scorers, Table 5 instruction count controls. The approach resembles a mutual verifier/generator self-training loop, not independent ground-truth validation.
srdf.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 3 p 7 under shared InternViT features reports baseline 78.6 SR/69.9 SPL→round 3 84.4/77.6 val-unseen. Final Table 7 p 9 test 85 SR/78 SPL, versus human 86/76: superior SPL is not superior human success. Table 5 p 8 compares 1, 3, 6, 12 instructions per path, showing saturation after 6; Table 11 p 21 navigator-filtered generator SPICE 25.2 versus 23.9 CLIP and 23.6 self-score. REVERIE/SOON results explicitly evaluate navigation, not grounding (§4.1). Verdict: strong data-quality evidence, but semantic fidelity is measured indirectly. Larger vision model, PanoGen and task-specific fine-tuning are confounders in cross-paper leaderboard comparisons.

Appendix Tables 14–18, pp 23–24, reports R4R nDTW 56.5/SDTW 44.6 and RxR-English nDTW 74.4/SDTW 66.3 on validation unseen, improving the cited route-fidelity baselines as well as endpoint success. REVERIE test SR 61.4 is accompanied by RGS 35.6, below GOAT 38.3, while RGSPL 27.1 slightly exceeds GOAT 26.7. Thus data scaling does not uniformly solve object grounding. Appendix qualitative claims about rare objects, OCR and outdoor scenes are examples, not controlled tests of those abilities.

gaussianmap.problem: Represent both geometry and open-set semantics for discrete VLN. Requires panoramic RGB-D, camera intrinsics/poses and graph candidate nodes; 3D representation alone does not turn this into continuous control.
gaussianmap.method: AUTHOR METHOD (§3 pp 3–5): back-project depth pixels to pseudo-lidar points, initialize anisotropic Gaussians with position, covariance, opacity and color, then refine through differentiable RGB/depth rendering. SAM2 masks identify coherent regions; CLIP produces 512-D region embeddings, mean-pooled to one scalar per region. A rendered scalar semantic attribute on each Gaussian is optimized to match these targets. Action features concatenate 3-D position, 3-D color and 1-D semantic code into 7-D vectors. Scene-wide, view-restricted and instance-restricted pooling feed language-conditioned transformer heads; map their scores to candidate waypoints and combine with traditional 2D action scores and topological memory. Navigation pretrains MLM/SAP/OG, then DAgger; map optimization uses RGB L1/SSIM, depth L1 and semantic L1. Reported 100k pretrain iterations batch 64, 25k finetuning batch 8; inference constructs map at each waypoint. Claimed 0.07s map construction is author-reported and should not be conflated with total SAM2/CLIP/navigation latency.
gaussianmap.novelty: Explicit Gaussian geometry plus semantic grouping and scene/view/instance action heads, relative to VER voxels and BEVBert top-down cells. It reuses a DUET-referenced topological/decision framework rather than establishing a wholly independent architecture (§3.5).
gaussianmap.results: PAPER EXPERIMENT: Table 2 p 6 reports R2R test 75 SR/65 SPL, versus BEVBert 73/62; REVERIE Table 1 val-unseen 53.59 SR/26.74 RGSPL and test 52.93/25.76. Test navigation SR is below some contemporary methods even when grounding improves. The evidence supports task utility, not retention of arbitrary CLIP semantics. DEDUCTION: mean-pooling a 512-D embedding is non-injective, so distinct vectors can share the same semantic scalar. Eq 12 sums three normalized distributions but labels the result [0, 1]; absent normalization it need not be a probability distribution. This notation/implementation ambiguity cannot be resolved without code.

uagm.problem: Use spatially localized uncertainty to guide RGB-D graph navigation under ambiguous geometry, semantics and appearance. Requires differentiable Gaussian reconstruction and known camera transforms; does not directly estimate calibrated action-error probabilities.
uagm.method:
AUTHOR METHOD (§3 pp 4–6): Semantic Gaussian Map initializes position 3, scale 3, quaternion 4, opacity 1, color 3 and semantic 3 attributes. Prune small/transparent Gaussians. Learn variational position/scale perturbations with an ELBO under Gaussian position and scale-relative uniform priors; aggregate posterior standard deviations for geometric uncertainty. Repeat for semantic offsets. Appearance score is logdet of each Gaussian block of an image-reconstruction Fisher/Gauss–Newton approximation (Eq 9). Concatenate three uncertainty scalars with 17 original attributes into 20-D Gaussian vectors, project to 768 dimensions, aggregate and fuse with instruction through transformer action scores/topological memory. Pretrain MLM/SAP/OG for 100k iterations batch 64, Adam 1e-4; DAgger 25k batch 8 learning rate 1e-5. Inference reconstructs map and uncertainty before predicting action.

Appendix B.1–B.2, PDF p 17, explicitly retains DUET’s 2D branch alongside the added 3D value branch. The 768-dimensional visual and text representations produce candidate distributions; pretraining uses masked-token NLL and expert-action NLL, adding target-object NLL for REVERIE. DAgger supplies shortest-path pseudo-expert labels. Appendix C.4 specifies a per-Gaussian block-diagonal, first-order-gradient outer-product approximation for Fisher information. A finite, well-conditioned log determinant still requires an explicit regularization/rank convention, which the unavailable code prevents checking.
uagm.novelty: Extends Gaussian scene representations with separate geometry/semantic perturbation variability and appearance sensitivity. Table 4 compares DUET, geometry-only, uncertainty-only and joint representations; Table 6 ablates uncertainty components. This is uncertainty-informed representation learning, not a proven Bayesian navigation policy.
uagm.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: R2R Table 2 p 8 gives test 76 SR/66 SPL, equal to VER in these rounded metrics; val-unseen 78/66. Table 4 p 9 lists REVERIE full-model SR 53.37, whereas headline Table 1 p 7 lists 56.37 with the same 37.65 RGS/27.01 RGSPL; preserve this internal discrepancy rather than choosing one silently. Table 5 pruning increases FPS from 11.2 to 15.5 at 42k primitives, but aggressive 35k harms SR. DEDUCTION: logdet Fisher can be negative or −∞ and is a sensitivity/precision quantity; interpreting it as nonnegative uncertainty-ellipsoid volume requires qualifications, regularization and possibly inverse information. Eq 8 approximation also requires small residuals. No calibration/error-prediction experiment in inspected tables establishes that higher score means larger decision error.

Appendix Table 8, PDF p 18, reports per-step time DUET 1.31s versus full UAGM 3.48s and MobileSAM UAGM 2.63s. Nearby text says the full method adds 1.35s, while the table difference is 2.17s; report table values separately. Table 11, p 19, labels five-run mean±standard deviation, confidence intervals and paired t-test p-values. The very small reported p-values warrant checking the statistical unit and raw paired runs before relying on them; no misconduct inference is made. Appendix E.2’s similar-looking renderings do not mathematically bound the neglected Hessian residual. E.3/Table 13 reports small gains when uncertainty maps are supplied to DUET, BEVBert and VER, which supports transferable signals but not calibrated probability estimates. E.4/Figure 7 gives concrete premature-stop examples: seeing a sofa before reaching it, and halting outside a room with a hidden target. E.4/Table 14 uses 20 selected scenes, so its 10/10 to 2/10 complex-scene result is not a representative benchmark estimate.

bevbert.title: BEVBert: Multimodal Map Pre-training for Language-guided Navigation
bevbert.problem: Panorama-only pretraining duplicates observations and makes local spatial relations implicit. BEVBert combines a global topology with a fine local ground-plane representation, assuming depth and pose or estimated depth.
bevbert.method:
AUTHOR METHOD (§3): CLIP patch features projected using depth/pose into a 21×21 metric grid of 0.5m cells, centered on the current agent; aggregate nearby visited nodes within a topology-order neighbourhood. Keep global visited/current/ghost graph nodes with panorama features. DUET-style graph-aware attention handles topology; a second cross-modal transformer handles cell features with polar location and navigability embeddings. Hybrid single-action prediction maps local cells to global node scores and gates local/global outputs (Eqs 3–5). MLM predicts masked words; masked semantic imagination (MSI) predicts 40-category multilabel semantics in masked cells with binary cross entropy (Eq 6). MSI is a training auxiliary, not an online future-state rollout. Alternate teacher/student forcing after pretraining. Pretrain 100k batch 64 then finetune 40k batch 16, 4 A100s, respectively about 10/20 hours. CE variant adds waypoint prediction and topology construction.

Appendix B, pp 13–15, samples MLM:HSAP:MSI at 5:5:1 for route-following tasks; REVERIE omits MSI and uses MLM:HSAP:MRC:OG at 1:1:1:1. Fine-tuning minimizes λL_teacher + L_student, with optional object grounding; λ=.2 for R2R/CE/REVERIE but .8 for RxR, whose non-shortest paths use nDTW-oriented pseudo-expert labels. Transformer text-branch attention is cut during fine-tuning to control expanding rollout memory. The estimated-depth ablation trains RedNet on training houses and retrains BEVBert with those estimates; it is not a zero-cost replacement at inference.
bevbert.novelty: Joint local metric/global topological pretraining, spatial embeddings and MSI. It explicitly inherits DUET GASA; hybrid representation differs from simply appending raw depth. Table 5 compares topology, metric and hybrid maps under sensed/estimated depth.
bevbert.results:
PAPER EXPERIMENT: R2R Table 1 p 6 test 73 SR/62 SPL versus DUET 69/59. REVERIE test 52.81 SR/22.09 RGSPL is nearly DUET 52.51/22.06 despite larger validation gains. Table 5 p 7 hybrid estimated-depth 74.67 SR/63.63 SPL versus sensed 74.88/63.60 suggests exact depth is not essential on that test. Fig 4 spatial/numerical-token slices degrade with increasing complexity even for BEVBert. Verdict: improves spatial representation, while complexity-conditioned language understanding remains partial; leaderboard comparisons must control CLIP, augmentation and sensor interfaces.

Appendix E, pp 15–17, explicitly records early deviations followed by excessive unsuccessful backtracking, loss of instruction-state tracking, ordinal-room ambiguity, and stopping at a kitchen counter after skipping a required turn. These failures persist despite a metric map and masked semantic imagination. Table 7, p 8, gives short-term-transformer FLOPs 4.5G for 11×11 cells, 15.2G for 21×21, and 32.7G for 31×31, showing that map refinement incurs a measurable cost.

gridmm.method: AUTHOR METHOD (§3 pp 4–6): store CLIP-B/32 grid features with absolute projected coordinates. At every action rotate/translate all history to the current egocentric frame. Set square extent to twice the maximum absolute coordinate and divide into fixed N×N cells. Within each cell, score feature-token relevance, max over instruction words, softmax over features, and weighted-pool into a 768-D cell token (Eqs 6–10). Combine map and trajectory memories, then cross-attend observation/history queries to instruction/history/map features. DUET-style dynamic fusion scores local views and global waypoints. Pretrain MLM/MVM/SAP plus historical-environment reasoning (HER), which predicts action without current panorama; DAgger uses graph shortest-route pseudo-expert. Inference retains all historical feature/coordinate pairs, so fixed map tokens do not mean fixed raw-history memory.
gridmm.novelty: Compared with BEVBert, global rather than local metric coverage and instruction-conditioned per-cell pooling; compared with DUET, explicit continuous geometry and history-only auxiliary prediction. HER is not a learned future simulator.

hamt.problem: Long navigation histories cannot be reconstructed reliably from a fixed recurrent state. HAMT receives the instruction, all previous panoramic observations/actions, and the current panorama, then predicts the next navigable direction or STOP. Its graph-navigation experiments assume viewpoint localization and candidate directions; those assumptions are distinct from low-level robot control.
hamt.method:
PDF pp 3–5: each panoramic view is encoded by a ViT; a panorama Transformer aggregates its K views, combining pooled panoramic context with the orientation-specific view. A temporal Transformer encodes the resulting history tokens, action directions, and step embeddings. A cross-modal Transformer jointly reasons over text, history, and current candidates. The hidden dimension is 768; reported configuration uses 9 language, 2 panorama, and 4 cross-modal layers. With t steps and K views, hierarchical attention costs O(tK²+t²), versus O(t²K²) for flattened history. This reduces attention cost but does not make memory constant. Pretraining combines masked language/region prediction, instruction–trajectory matching, single-action CE, action-angle squared error, and spatial-relation regression. In the latter, the target is the relative heading/elevation between two views and masking prevents trivial copying. Fine-tuning minimizes imitation CE plus an A3C policy/value/entropy objective; the supervised action term is −Σt log π(a*t|W, Ht, Ot). The reported imitation weight is 0.2 and discount 0.9. Training first freezes the ViT for 200k steps (4 P100), then updates it for 20k steps (20 V100); fine-tuning is 100k steps with batch 8. Inference greedily selects a candidate from the history-conditioned logits without search.

Supplement A.1 (p 1; extended p 15) makes the alignment objectives explicit. For word vocabulary size V, an MLP maps a masked token h_i in R^768 to a V-way distribution and minimizes token negative log likelihood. For each masked visual token, a 1000-way ImageNet teacher distribution P_i supplies soft-target cross entropy −sum_j P_ij log Q_ij, equal to KL up to teacher entropy. ITM scores text-CLS elementwise multiplied by history-CLS, both 768-dimensional, and uses a five-way contrastive objective with one positive, two other-trajectory negatives and two temporal shuffles. Supplement B.3 samples MLM:MRM:ITM:SAP:SAR:SPREL as 5:2:2:1:1:1. For R2R-Back, training requires two stops at distinct stages; success requires visiting the original endpoint before returning, and SPL uses the full reference route length. Ordinary start-goal geodesic SPL would be degenerate for this task.
hamt.novelty: Explicit hierarchical history encoding and end-to-end visual adaptation are the principal mechanisms. The paper introduces R2R-Back and R2R-Last to probe history requirements. It does not introduce global graph action selection: history tokens influence a local action policy. Table 2 isolates the hierarchy with the same ResNet feature family; Table 3 separates proxy training, ViT features, and visual fine-tuning.
hamt.results:
AUTHOR EXPERIMENT: Table 2 p 7 reports hierarchical-from-scratch SR 54.4±0.4 versus recurrent 52.2±0.7; Table 3 p 8 shows much larger changes from pretraining and vision adaptation (ResNet no pretraining 54.4 SR; proxy-trained ResNet 63.5; ViT 64.4; end-to-end 65.7). Table 4 gives IL-only 57.2, RL-only 63.5, combined 65.7 SR. VERDICT: explicit history helps under matched features, but attributing the entire headline gain to memory would be incorrect. The cost analysis and limited trajectory lengths do not establish scalability to lifelong navigation.

Supplement C.1/Table 2 (extended Table 11) reports 2349 R2R unseen instructions on one P100: RecBERT 69s, HAMT 104s, and the no-text-to-vision variant 76s. This establishes a measured tradeoff for that setup, not constant history cost. Supplement D.1 compares a reimplemented PREVALENT without history, but also removes ITM, so the 57.5 versus 52.7 SPL contrast does not isolate history alone despite the later phrase “same proxy tasks.” D.4 finds single-stage end-to-end training inferior at the tested schedule (SPL 53.5 versus 56.5 without end-to-end training). REVERIE grounding remains weaker than competing object features; the authors hypothesize that R2R-tuned ViT features transfer poorly to object grounding. Failure captions identify unusual spatial orientation and object recognition errors.

Main Table 7, PDF p 9, compares models retrained on the R2R-Back task: unseen HAMT SR 57.2/SPL 53.1 versus RecBERT 41.1/37.7. This targeted return-to-start task supplies stronger memory evidence than a general R2R leaderboard difference. Table 6 gives R4R nDTW 50.3 versus 45.1 for reimplemented RecBERT. Table 8/p 10 reports CVDN goal progress 5.58m on test; it is not an SPL percentage.

vlnbert.title: VLN BERT: A Recurrent Vision-and-Language BERT for Navigation
vlnbert.problem: Adapt pretrained vision–language Transformers to sequential, partially observed action selection without an additional LSTM navigation backbone. This is the recurrent VLN-BERT paper by Hong et al., not the earlier discriminative VLN-BERT path-ranking paper.
vlnbert.method: PDF §3 pp 3–5: encode the instruction once and use its CLS output as initial state s_0∈R^d. At each step a Transformer consumes recurrent state st−1 and current panoramic candidates, attending to fixed language features. Text and visual attention summaries are multiplied elementwise and concatenated with the raw state before projection (Eq 12); the selected action angle is incorporated into the next state (Eq 13). Attention from the state to visual candidates supplies the action distribution. REVERIE additionally predicts the target object and adapts state refinement. OSCAR and PREVALENT initializations are separate variants; the PREVALENT implementation adapts its cross-modal architecture for recurrent state+vision inputs. Eq 14 combines actor-critic RL with supervised imitation CE; the scalar policy term uses discounted advantage and the supervised term −logπ(a*t). Object grounding adds CE on REVERIE. Reported AdamW learning rate is 1e−5; R2R 300k steps/batch 16 and REVERIE 200k/batch 8 on one 2080Ti. Inference recurrently updates the state and greedily acts, rather than ranking complete paths.
vlnbert.novelty: The contribution is recurrent reuse of a pretrained multimodal Transformer and state-directed attention for navigation. Initialization and architecture are jointly important: Table 1 compares random, OSCAR, and PREVALENT variants. It should not be grouped as a general-purpose instruction-following VLM with training-free inference.

airbert.problem: Reduce the domain gap between generic web image–text pretraining and indoor instruction navigation without requiring new embodied human demonstrations. The BnB corpus uses approximately 140k rental listings, 1.4M images and 0.7M captions; images in one listing need not form a physically traversable trajectory.
airbert.method: PDF pp 3–5: clean rental images/captions, sample 4–7-image pseudo-paths from a listing, merge room views, concatenate captions, insert uncaptained views, and create instructions by template noun substitution or generation. A ViLBERT-style two-stream model encodes language tokens and visual regions with image separators. Besides masked token/region prediction, the shuffling objective contrasts a matched trajectory–instruction pair against shuffled order negatives. In Eq 3, for scalar compatibility sθ(V, W), L=−log[exp sθ(V, W)/(exp sθ(V, W)+Σn exp sθ(Vn−, Wn−))]; the contrast concerns ordering compatibility, not physical transition validity. The model supports two distinct downstream uses: discriminative reranking of explored complete trajectories, and initialization of recurrent VLN-BERT for action generation. These inference protocols must remain separated.
airbert.novelty: In-domain non-embodied pretraining and order-sensitive shuffling are the mechanisms. The synthetic-path construction supplies scale but sacrifices measured geometry. prevalent.problem: Pretrain representations using navigation-specific image–instruction–action triplets to transfer across embodied instruction tasks. Unlike later history-aware policies, its pretraining action prediction conditions on a current observation and instruction.
prevalent.method:
PDF pp 3–5: 36 panoramic ResNet view features (2048 visual+128 angle dimensions) are projected into a 768-dimensional Transformer with 9 language, 1 vision and 3 cross-modal layers. Masked language modeling hides 15% of words; action prediction uses a CLS representation to classify the next panoramic direction. For triplet (W, V, a), L_AP=−log pθ(a|W, V); MLM is cross entropy of masked words conditioned on unmasked language and views. These objectives do not explicitly supervise temporal memory. Training uses 104k human-derived triplets and approximately 6.482M synthetic triplets from 1.02M generated instructions, totaling 6.582M. Reported pretraining uses 8 V100 GPUs, 20 epochs, AdamW at 5e−5. Downstream R2R integrates pretrained language features into an EnvDrop/LSTM agent; this differs from later recurrent VLN-BERT, which recurrently uses the multimodal backbone. Inference follows the trained downstream policy.

Section 6.5, PDF p 8, clarifies that most downstream experiments use frozen pretrained features for computational efficiency. R2R additionally uses a two-stage adaptation that unfreezes cross-attention after feature-based training. These schedules should not be collapsed into a single claim that all pretrained parameters are always updated.
prevalent.novelty: Navigation-specific multimodal/action pretraining is the contribution, rather than a new online map or world model. Transfer across R2R, CVDN, HANNA supports usefulness of the representation; the data scale and downstream policy remain material parts of the result.
prevalent.results:
AUTHOR EXPERIMENT: Table 1 p 6 reports test SR 54/SPL 51 for the single-instruction setting and 59/56 for the multiple-instruction setting. They are separate protocols. VERDICT: effective task-oriented pretraining, but its state-independent pretraining cannot establish history-sensitive reasoning and synthetic instruction quality is not independently certified.

Table 5, PDF p 8, gives test SR/SPL 54/51 for two-stage R2R adaptation versus 52/49 using fixed features. Table 4 shows small and nonuniform increments from adding action pretraining on CVDN: for all dialog text and mixed supervision, goal progress is 3.15 versus 3.14 with multimodal MLM alone. The much larger comparison against ordinary BERT cannot be attributed solely to the action objective. HANNA Table 3/p 7 increases unseen SR from 47.45 to 52.91 while assistance requests also rise from 5.8 to 6.6.

speakerfollower.problem: Human navigation instructions are scarce and an instruction-conditioned follower may choose routes whose visual content does not explain the instruction. A learned reverse-direction speaker supplies both additional training instructions and a route-compatibility score.
speakerfollower.method:
PDF pp 3–6: train an LSTM speaker PS(d|r) on human route–description pairs; generate descriptions for 178k sampled shortest routes in training environments; train a follower PF(r|d) on augmented data then fine-tune on human data. The follower attends over language and 36-view panoramic features and selects neighboring viewpoints or STOP. A state-factored search collects 40 completed candidate routes. Final selection is argmaxr PS(d|r)^λ PF(r|d)^(1−λ), equivalently λlogPS+(1−λ)logPF; λ is near 1. The inspected code evaluates 0 and 0.95 weights and can standardize scores. State-factored search merges candidates by physical state despite history-dependent LSTM states; therefore it is approximate. The physical traversal needed to obtain candidate observations must count in trajectory length.

Section 4.1, PDF pp 6–7, specifies student forcing: sample follower actions and supervise the shortest-path action from the resulting state. Speaker maximum-likelihood training uses token cross entropy. The follower trains for 50k iterations on generated instructions and then 20k on human instructions; image ResNet features are fixed. The reported inference mixture uses λ=0.95.
speakerfollower.novelty: The same reverse instruction-generation model is used for both data augmentation and pragmatic inference. Panorama-level neighbor actions also change the action abstraction relative to the original low-level R2R baseline. These are separable sources of improvement, so the method is not merely a speaker loss added to an otherwise identical baseline.

These are separate resource protocols. VERDICT: augmentation, pragmatic reranking and action abstraction each contribute. selfmonitoring.problem: An agent needs to estimate whether its movement advances instruction completion and to detect deterioration before committing to a wrong branch. The paper estimates progress using supervised distance-to-goal targets rather than human labels of clause completion.
selfmonitoring.method:
PDF pp 3–5: a co-grounding LSTM attends to current panoramic views and instruction words. Its progress monitor combines prior hidden state, current memory cell, grounded visual context, and the vector of text-attention weights to predict scalar p̂t∈[−1, 1] using tanh. The target is pt=(d_0−dt)/d_0, overridden to 1 when dt≤3m; it can be negative when moving farther from the goal. Training uses weighted action CE and squared progress error. Although the PDF’s printed Eq 6 has a problematic negative sign on the MSE term, inspected code positively adds λMSE+(1−λ)CE; the implementation therefore minimizes squared error. At inference the monitor weights search candidates and can trigger backtracking when predicted progress decreases. Thus a progress monitor plus rollback is already established prior art.

Supplement PDF p 14 specifies 2176-dimensional view features (2048 ResNet plus 128 tiled angles), 512-dimensional recurrent states, a maximum of 80 instruction tokens, and a 592-to-1 progress projection combining hidden features with attention weights. Adam uses learning rate 1e−4 and batch 64; beam size is 15. The supplement describes physically logging and connecting searched trajectories for challenge submission.
selfmonitoring.novelty: Auxiliary progress estimation jointly regularizes visual–language grounding and supplies an inference heuristic. The progress signal is distance based; an attention alignment visualization does not prove that the monitor represents semantic instruction completion.

regretful.problem: Recover from mistaken local actions while avoiding repeated oscillation between previously visited viewpoints. The method extends the self-monitoring agent with a learned forward-versus-rollback decision and node-specific progress memory.
regretful.method: PDF §4 pp 3–5: compute progress p̂t and its difference Δpt=p̂t−p̂t−1. A learned 2-way softmax gate mixes forward embedding mf (instruction/current state) with rollback embedding mb (previous navigable direction): m=αfmf+αbmb. Progress values are detached before the gate, so action-loss gradients do not reshape the monitor through this path. A dictionary stores each visited node’s last progress; candidate features concatenate the difference between current progress and the stored value, tiled to balance feature scale. Unvisited nodes receive marker 1 and STOP 0. A post-rollback mask prevents immediate oscillation. Train with action CE, positive progress MSE, and entropy regularization βΣaπa logπa (β=.01, negative entropy encourages exploration); inference greedily selects an action. Memory is keyed by exact viewpoint identity, a simulator-provided assumption.
regretful.novelty: Learned rollback mixing plus persistent per-node progress markers extends earlier heuristic rollback. Neither storing visited progress nor using progress changes as a recovery trigger is new to a prospective 2027 proposal.

tacticalrewind.problem: Local navigation policies need a systematic means to leave an unproductive branch and compare plausible goal locations without committing permanently to the first STOP. FAST treats frontier choice and final goal ranking as distinct decisions.
tacticalrewind.method: PDF §2/Algorithm 1 pp 3–5: maintain frontier queue QF of partial routes/actions scored by exploration heuristic L, and candidate queue QC of possible completed routes scored by goal function G. Exploitation follows the local best action until confusion/loops; exploration selects the best frontier. A visited transition graph supports physical backtracking. L may aggregate raw action logits rather than log-softmax; G combines progress, speaker likelihood and path-score statistics through a trained reranker. Short search stops on a local stopping criterion; long search runs a fixed expansion budget. Every visited location can become a final goal candidate. Raw-logit accumulation avoids one softmax-normalization artifact discussed in the paper, but is not theoretically calibrated: adding an arbitrary state-dependent constant to all logits preserves the action distribution while changing summed-logit route ranking. This is a mathematical invariance counterexample, not an executed benchmark result.
tacticalrewind.novelty: Explicit separation of exploration and goal selection, organized backtracking, and plug-in search over existing followers. It directly anticipates proposals to decouple movement from stopping or rerank visited goal candidates; a new contribution must go beyond that abstraction.

rcm.problem: Use both goal-reaching reinforcement and route–instruction consistency to train a navigator, then adapt using unlabeled instructions in additional environments. Access to unseen environments during adaptation is a different evaluation regime from zero-shot unseen-scene generalization.
rcm.method: PDF pp 3–5: a recurrent reasoning navigator attends to instruction words and then to visual candidates. A fixed cross-modal matching critic estimates length-normalized instruction likelihood given an executed trajectory using a reverse sequence model. Supervised action-CE warm-start is followed by REINFORCE with extrinsic distance-progress/goal reward and intrinsic critic reward; γ=.95. For trajectory τ and instruction W, the policy term is −Σt logπθ(at|ht, W)At, where At includes return from these rewards. Self-supervised imitation learning (SIL) samples routes for unlabeled instructions, retains high-critic-score trajectories in replay, and imitates them. Eq 16’s reward-weighted objective and Eq 17’s simplified imitation update should not be described as algebraically identical without the authors’ approximation. Reported Adam rates are 1e−4 supervised and 1e−5 RL/SIL; ResNet is frozen and GloVe is fine-tuned. Inference uses the resulting trained navigator, not online gradient-free VLM prompting.
rcm.novelty: Cycle-style matching reward and self-supervised route replay combine language consistency with goal reinforcement. The critic is a learned proxy, not an independent semantic oracle; self-training may inherit its preferences.

r2r.problem: Define visually grounded natural-language navigation in realistic indoor panoramas. Matterport 3D Simulator uses 90 buildings, approximately 10,800 viewpoints and 194,400 RGB-D images; a graph discretizes traversable locations, so the benchmark does not directly test collision control, continuous localization, or dynamic obstacles.
r2r.method:
PDF pp 3–6: weighted undirected navigation edges are checked by ray tracing/manual inspection, generally between viewpoints within 5m (average spacing 2.25m). R2R samples 7,189 shortest paths of 4–6 edges and longer than 5m and collects 3 instructions per path:21,567 instructions averaging 29 words. Annotators are explicitly told that exact path following is not necessary if the goal is reached. The original baseline is an attention sequence-to-sequence LSTM using ResNet 152 image features and previous action, choosing left/right/up/down 30-degree rotations, forward to a visible neighbor, or STOP. This differs from later panoramic graph-neighbor action abstractions. Evaluation measures endpoint graph distance, success within 3m, and oracle success at the closest visited location, ignoring final orientation. OSR and SR therefore distinguish visiting from stopping, but their difference alone does not identify why stopping failed.

Section 5.2, PDF p 7, trains per-step action cross entropy with the next shortest-path action from the current pose as target. Teacher forcing visits demonstration states; student forcing samples policy actions and relabels the visited states. The language and policy LSTMs each have 512 hidden units, word embeddings 256 dimensions, and action embeddings 32. Adam uses batch 100, dropout .5 and weight decay. Test decoding is greedy; the submitted test model uses both training and validation data, which must be separated from models used to report validation performance.
r2r.novelty: A realistic photo-based simulator, connected navigation graph, human route descriptions, and held-out-building evaluation established the VLN task. Endpoint-oriented annotation is an intentional benchmark property, so instruction-path faithfulness requires additional metrics/datasets rather than assuming all goal shortcuts violate R2R’s original contract.

crossmodalmap.problem: CM² addresses VLN-CE with a 90-degree RGB-D view, ground-truth pose, noiseless 0.25m forward/15-degree turns and STOP. It predicts a language-conditioned local semantic map and a complete waypoint sequence, then delegates physical control to DD-PPO. Ground-truth pose and pretrained controller experience are material resource assumptions.
crossmodalmap.method: §3 pp 3–5: project depth into a 192×192 occupancy grid with 5 cm cells; separately segment RGB. BERT produces M×128 text features, while a truncated ResNet 18 encodes the map into N×128 tokens. Cross-attention H=softmax((YWq)(XWk)ᵀ/√128)XWv uses map queries and text keys/values. Two stacked U-Nets predict occupancy then 27-category semantics, including unseen regions, trained with pixel CE against simulator semantic maps. A second cross-modal network predicts k waypoint heatmaps P̂∈R^(k×u×v) and traversed-waypoint labels, conditioned on the start heatmap. Lwp=Σi bi||P̂i−Pi||² plus waypoint-coverage CE, where bi masks waypoints outside the local map. Total loss combines map and waypoint losses in one backward pass. At inference choose the waypoint after the one closest to current pose; DD-PPO reaches it. Stop when close to the final predicted waypoint and heatmap confidence exceeds a threshold. This is language-conditioned map hallucination plus replanning, not an action-conditioned recurrent future-state simulator.
crossmodalmap.novelty: Language informs both unobserved map completion and path prediction. Table 3 isolates map attention, supporting better map/waypoint accuracy. Unlike pre-exploration topological planners, CM² builds predictions online, but it assumes true pose and privileged map-label supervision during training.

weakmap.problem: WS-MGMap addresses loss of object attributes in category-only maps and weak correspondence between map regions and instruction objects in continuous navigation. It assumes RGB-D, metric projection and simulator-provided training geometry/semantics.
weakmap.method:
§3 pp 4–6: project 64-channel latent U-Net segmentation features into a 100×100 grid with 12 cm cells. A hallucination module predicts 27-category semantic occupancy; fuse fine-grained and semantic features by convolutions. A GRU encodes RGB/depth/map history, attends to BiLSTM instruction features, then computes a spatial distribution P̂ over map cells. Weak target P=softmax(P′), P′k=(dmax−dk)/(dmax−dmin), is based on distance dk to the demonstration path, not annotated object locations. Optimize KL(P||P̂). The attended map, text and first GRU state feed a second GRU; linear heads regress a 2D waypoint and scalar progress. A LAW-style expert chooses a point 3m along the shortest route to the nearest reference waypoint; DD-PPO executes low-level actions and STOP fires when progress>.8. L=Lsemantic+10Llocalization+10Lprogress+10Lwaypoint, with squared regression errors; teacher-forcing on 150k augmented examples is followed by DAgger. Frozen segmentation/controller and 2 V100 GPUs over 3 days are reported. Waypoints refresh every 3 steps.

Appendix A–B, pp 14–15, clarifies that fine-grained, semantic and fused maps actually have different tensor resolutions despite the shared m×m notation in the main paper: fine map 64×100×100, semantic map 27×48×48, fused map 256×24×24. Adam uses 2.5e−4; teacher forcing runs 30 epochs, followed by 10 DAgger collections of 5000 trajectories and 4 epochs per collection, with oracle-action probability 0.5^n. The released trainer regresses bounded 2D waypoints using MSE, not categorical primitive-action CE.
weakmap.novelty: Fuses latent attribute features with hallucinated category maps and path-derived weak localization. The weak target encourages path proximity; calling it verified object grounding would exceed its supervision. Eq 3 describes cosine similarity but prints an unnormalized projected dot product; the inspected attention implementation uses dot-product-style attention, so normalization assumptions should be checked before reusing the equation.

goat.problem: GOAT targets dataset-dependent visual/language/history shortcuts in DUET-family navigation. It assumes room/keyword confounders and latent style/trajectory confounders in a structural causal model; these are modeling assumptions, not variables randomized by its benchmark.
goat.method:
§4 pp 3–6: extract RoBERTa direction/landmark dictionaries and CLIP room dictionaries labeled by BLIP VQA. Back-door-inspired features add fx(x)+Σz wzfz(z), using empirical frequencies or query-dependent attention weights. Front-door-inspired modules attend both current-input features and K-means-selected global training features, then sum the resulting expectations. A sigmoid gate mixes adjusted and original features. Language, local panorama and global/history features enter DUET-style dual-scale fusion and action CE. Contrastive cross-modal feature pooling uses normalized bidirectional batch InfoNCE between pooled language and local/global/fused embeddings, temperature t; it pretrains the representations used to build dictionaries. Reported 6 text/2 panorama/3 cross layers, CLIP-B/16, METER initialization, batch 12 (5 for RxR/SOON), learning rate 2e−5, max 100k; dynamic speaker augmentation is also used. Inference reads learned dictionaries and predicts graph actions; it does not perform physical randomized interventions.

Section 5.1, PDF p 6, specifies pretraining for up to 300k iterations with AdamW, batch 48 and learning rate 5e−5 on one V100, using MLM, SAP and contrastive pooling, plus object grounding for REVERIE/SOON. EnvEdit visual augmentation and external synthetic datasets are also used. The 74 keyword classes, 50 room classes and InfoNCE temperature 1 are part of the experimental configuration.
goat.novelty: The engineering contribution is dictionary-conditioned multimodal feature adjustment, contrastive pooling, and gated integration on a dual-scale graph backbone. The author’s claim of unbiased causal effects is stronger than evidence: front-door identification requires no unblocked X→M confounding, all causal X→Y paths mediated by M, and back-door blocking between M, Y by X. These assumptions are not established for learned attention/dictionaries; query-dependent weighting is not automatically the marginal P(z), and residual original-feature paths persist. Benchmark gains support useful regularization, not identification.
goat.results:

VERDICT: compelling multimodal regularizer baseline for future causal claims, but one should test controlled counterfactual invariance and preserve task-relevant direction/landmark effects rather than treating all frequent keywords as removable nuisance.

Tables 1–2, PDF p 7, report R2R test SR 74.57/SPL 64.94 and REVERIE test RGS 38.32/RGSPL 26.70. hsgm.title: Bridging the 2D-3D Gap: A Hierarchical Semantic-Geometric Map for Vision Language Navigation
hsgm.problem: Training-free task adaptation using a pretrained VLM to choose semantically meaningful, geometrically reachable waypoints. Inputs include front/left/right RGB-D and pose; GPT-5 and YOLO-E remain pretrained components, so training-free does not mean no learned perception or no API cost.
hsgm.method: §3 pp 3–6: backproject RGB-D into a geometric point cloud, segment open-vocabulary instances with YOLO-E, and merge consistent 3D instances. Build dense global and sparse local waypoint graphs after cylinder-occupancy, distance, obstacle-clearance and reachability checks; stairs use surface-normal/tilted-plane filtering. Rasterize geometry, object categories, path and completed-subtask locations into BEV, and annotate current image with waypoint IDs. A VLM decomposes instruction into ordered subtasks with pending/in-progress/done states. Each subtask has at most 3 motion directives and a stated termination condition. The VLM selects a waypoint/turn/STOP; A* over the observed graph minimizes sum of edge Euclidean lengths and converts the path into rotations/forward motions. The paper specifies two consecutive STOP predictions for final completion; the released code retains the first STOP flag across intervening motion, as detailed below. A timeout returns to the subtask start for another attempt. No VLN training objective is optimized; runtime updates maps and prompt history.
hsgm.novelty: Geometric waypoint validation, rasterized hierarchical maps, structured subtask management and decoupled A* control are integrated into a zero-shot VLM pipeline. Double-confirmed stopping, semantic progress bookkeeping, and timeout backtracking are explicit prior art for recovery proposals.
hsgm.results: AUTHOR EXPERIMENT: Table 1 p 6 full R2R-CE val-unseen 47.9 SR/32.8 SPL; RxR-CE 41.8/25.1/54.9 nDTW on 500 random English episodes. Ablations use a separate 300-episode R2R subset: full 51 SR, without subtasks 42.1, without structured CoT 34.0. Table 4 reports backtracking triggered 18.3%/19.0%, recovered-episode success 30.8%/26.8%; this is conditional success, not causal recovery gain against a matched no-backtracking control. The A* ablation uses straight-line movement, so its gain does not isolate semantics from collision handling. VERDICT: strong practical baseline with expensive proprietary inference and privileged sensors; matched VLM/backbone/episode comparisons are essential.

ivln.problem: Iterative VLN asks whether a robot can exploit persistent experience across sequential instructions in the same building. Episodes form tours rather than independent resets. The protocol includes an oracle correction to the true goal and transport to the next start while the agent passively observes; this is meaningful additional supervision/experience.
ivln.method: §3 pp 3–4 constructs tours by approximately solving an asymmetric traveling-salesperson ordering over existing R2R paths, using connectivity partitions and a Lin–Kernighan heuristic. t-nDTW computes exp(−DTW(Rtour, Qtour)/(|Rtour|dth)), forbids cross-episode alignment by infinite costs, excludes oracle transport, then averages tours weighted by episode count. This discourages sacrificing one episode for unlimited exploration. TourHAMT keeps up to 50 previous steps with boundary tokens; TourCMA retains a visual GRU state; pooling variants store max-pooled latent history. MAP-CMA projects semantics/occupancy into a persistent metric map, crops 14×64×64 tensors, encodes to 128×4×4, and replaces CMA RGB inputs. Training distinguishes episodic/iterative/known maps and ground-truth/RedNet semantics. Latent baselines use teacher forcing with episode-truncated gradients; map models additionally use augmented pretraining, progress loss and DAgger. Inference persists maps across episodes but resets instruction-specific state.
ivln.novelty: Persistent multi-episode benchmark and tour-level metric, with controlled memory-reset variants. The main scientific result is that naive longer latent history can hurt while explicit map reuse helps; it is not evidence that all unstructured memories fundamentally fail.

For predicted semantics, iterative-map training/evaluation reaches 35 SR/32 SPL/47 tour-nDTW, while training/evaluating with a fully known map reaches 31/28/44. marval.title: A New Path: Scaling Vision-and-Language Navigation with Synthetic Instructions and Imitation Learning
marval.problem: Test whether higher-quality, larger synthetic navigation datasets plus imitation learning can replace complicated RL pipelines. The main challenge is scaling both environments and grounded instructions, while retaining the language style of the evaluation dataset.
marval.method: §3–4 pp 3–6: a randomly initialized mT5-style encoder concatenates instruction, pooled panoramic/action history, current 36 views and candidates with learned modality/relative-position biases. Fixed 640D MURAL-large features inherit large external image–text pretraining. Pretraining combines masked language, 20-bin progress classification, candidate-constrained action CE and 37-class direction/STOP CE; constrained and unconstrained logits are equally mixed. Fine-tuning updates only word embeddings, using behavioral cloning or one effective DAgger iteration. Experts follow the next reference action when on path, shortest-to-goal when the reference is shortest, and shortest-back-to-reference otherwise. Marky generates 3.2M multilingual instructions on 491 Gibson scenes; graph construction combines learned reachability, geodesic/Euclidean ratio and MST connectivity. SE3DS creates 200 perturbed panorama variants per Matterport scene. Model pretraining reaches 5.14M iterations, batch 128 (>650M state examples). Pre-exploration additionally self-trains on evaluation environments and is a separate privileged regime.
marval.novelty: Large multilingual Marky-Gibson data and a deliberately simple, pure-imitation Transformer demonstrate the importance of instruction quality, environment diversity and distribution correction. It is outside DUET’s dual-branch architecture, although it shares panoramic graph tasks and history pooling.

navillm.problem: Unify instruction navigation, object localization, trajectory summarization, 3D QA and held-out EQA within a multimodal language model. Multi-task transfer is central; a model trained on several embodied datasets is distinct from an untouched general VLM used zero-shot.
navillm.method:
Paper §3–4 pp 3–5: frozen EVA-CLIP-Large 428M gives per-view CLS features; a 2-layer 1024D Transformer fuses views plus angle/GPS information; projections align them to Vicuna-7B. Prompts contain Task, indexed Observation, indexed History and Output Hint. Paper describes generation of view/object IDs, summaries or answers using unified token CE, L=−Σj log pθ(yj|prompt, y<j). History stores selected-view representations. Pretraining 10k steps and multi-task fine-tuning 5k, batch 64, Adam 3e−5, 8 A100 GPUs for about 80 hours; teacher/student forcing alternate. Data includes CVDN, SOON, R2R, REVERIE, ScanQA, augmentation and 23k LLaVA examples. Test uses greedy generation except temperature .01 for SOON/REVERIE. RELEASED-CODE QUALIFICATION: nav_model.py additionally uses global graph candidate embeddings and visited masks, merges local embeddings, permutes candidates, then applies a classifier head to LLM CLS hidden states for navigation logits. Thus the release contains DUET-derived graph infrastructure and the action path is not simply unrestricted textual ID generation.

The released implementation differs materially from the paper’s uniform generation description: train.py 229 creates CrossEntropyLoss(ignore_index, reduction=sum), and tasks/agents/mp3d_agent.py 734–756 applies it to navigation candidate logits and teacher action indices. Separate QA and summarization branches apply language-model generation losses at 865 and 901. Therefore, the inspected released navigation branch is an LLM-conditioned graph classifier with separate generative tasks, not solely next-token generation of a view ID.
navillm.novelty: Schema-unified embodied multi-task adaptation of an LLM, with transfer to held-out tasks. The contribution is broader than a stronger R2R policy. Paper-versus-release differences should be resolved before using it as a supposedly graph-free VLM baseline.

VERDICT: useful generalist baseline, not universal dominance over specialized models.

Supplement pp 1–3 gives task history caps (15 for R2R/REVERIE, 30 for CVDN, 20 for SOON), excludes 849 EQA examples, and supplies candidate(0)=STOP prompts. Its SOON count is 27.8k in Table 3 versus 2780 in the text, an apparent factor-ten reporting discrepancy. Schema ablations aggregate heterogeneous metric units; that aggregate should not be interpreted as a calibrated universal navigation score.

Table 5, PDF p 8, shows that extra pretraining does not improve every task: relative to multi-task training with a pretrained LLM, adding the pretraining stage increases R2R SPL 58→59 but lowers REVERIE SPL 36.63→35.68 and ScanQA exact match 23.3→22.1. navrag.problem: Generate diverse user-demand-oriented goal instructions beyond the narrow style of trajectory speakers trained on small R2R/REVERIE corpora. NavRAG is primarily a data-generation system; its downstream DUET does not perform LLM retrieval at navigation time.
navrag.method: §3 pp 3–5 builds a bottom-up scene description tree from object/view to viewpoint, semantic-connectivity zone, and house. GPT-4o-mini describes 6 views per viewpoint; zones grow by connectivity plus LLM semantic membership, rather than Euclidean clustering alone. Scene context and 20 manually specified user profiles generate rough daily tasks, then top-down zone→viewpoint→view retrieval refines the instruction and selects a target. A graph planner supplies the path. Training data has 2,115,019 instructions across 861 training scenes (800 HM3D + 61 MP3D); separate 11 MP3D validation scenes are annotated for evaluation. Graph generation follows ScaleVLN. The trained navigation model uses DUET imitation/pretraining machinery, with object-box features removed in fairer downstream comparisons. No new inference loss is introduced by the data pipeline; instruction quality rests on a chain of model-generated descriptions/targets.
navrag.novelty: User-demand simulation and hierarchical retrieval grounded in scene connectivity expand language diversity relative to route-to-text speakers. This does not certify factual correctness: the authors’ Limitations explicitly state no effective correctness evaluator and viewpoint-level, not precise object-level, target annotations.

AUTHOR EXPERIMENT: Table 2 p 7 DUET trained on NavRAG achieves NavRAG 30.7 SR/25.4 SPL versus ScaleVLN-REVERIE 17.4/11.9; transfer to REVERIE 36.1/24.9 is a distinct setting. Table 3 p 8 matched no-object-box fine-tuning yields 57.3 SR/42.0 SPL versus ScaleVLN 55.9/40.6. Table 4 generator ablations change both training and validation generation processes (GraphRAG→GraphRAG versus NavRAG→NavRAG), so navigation differences do not isolate annotation correctness under a fixed test distribution. VERDICT: useful diversity/transfer evidence with explicitly unresolved semantic validation; prose task requests to manipulate objects are evaluated only as navigation.

The released shortest-path conversion imposes a goal-oriented route prior even though user-demand language is broad. Demand diversity and route-following fidelity are separate claims; this dataset is not a replacement for non-shortest-path RxR/R4R controls.

roomtour3d.problem: Extract useful indoor navigation supervision from real room-tour videos, avoiding the lack of measured motion in unordered rental images and the limited scene diversity of simulator annotations. Video motion still does not automatically provide valid alternative robot actions.
roomtour3d.method: §3 pp 3–5: sample video frames every 2 seconds; BLIP-2 predicts 16 room types with temporal smoothing; RAM tags objects, GroundingDINO boxes them, DepthAnything estimates depth. Text templates combine object category, relative direction/distance and room labels; GPT-4-Turbo turns frame sequences into trajectory descriptions. COLMAP reconstructs clips sampled 3 fps, 100 seconds with 10 second overlaps, merging reconstructions sharing>3 frames. Turning/revisited-location candidates are selected using orientation/cosine changes, NMS and DBSCAN; actual continuation is positive and strongly different orientations supply negatives. Dataset totals 200k instructions, 17k action-enriched trajectories, 1847 scenes. NaviLLM first learns trajectory summarization with token CE, then candidate-action prediction using action-enriched histories; human/simulator multi-task data remains in the regular supervised setting. Zero-shot-transfer variant removes simulator action/geometric training but still learns from RoomTour 3D actions.
roomtour3d.novelty: Real-video object/motion/geometry annotation and action-candidate mining, rather than a new backbone. Compared with AirBERT, ordered video and reconstructed geometry provide stronger motion evidence; reconstructed candidate views still differ from online reachable-neighbor observations.

topologicalplanning.title: Topological Planning with Transformers for Vision-and-Language Navigation
topologicalplanning.problem: Separate semantic global planning from low-level control using a topological map built by the agent. Each environment is explicitly explored along ten trajectories before instruction execution. Mapping uses RGB-D panoramas, heading and ground-truth odometry; navigation subsequently uses learned localization.
topologicalplanning.method: Section 3, PDF pp 3–6: sparsify and merge exploration graphs using reachability estimates. Nodes store globally oriented panoramas; edges encode eight directions and three distance bins. A message-passing GNN encodes nodes, edges and global context, followed by map, language and cross-modal Transformer layers. The planner selects a node sequence y with p(y|G, L)=Πt p(yt|y<t, G, L); learned trajectory-position embeddings distinguish selected and unselected nodes. Node/STOP classification uses cross entropy and AdamW. A separately DAgger-trained controller receives previous, current and subgoal panoramas and predicts one of 24 heading sectors plus a scalar distance. A Gaussian bias toward the previous direction suppresses oscillation from perceptual aliasing. Low-level actions turn 15 degrees or move 0.25m. Predicted distance determines when to advance to the next planned node. The full plan is computed before execution, distinct from online exploration.
topologicalplanning.novelty: Cross-modal global planning on an automatically constructed topology is combined with modular visual localization and control. Crucial stopping prior art appears in Section 4.1, p 6: categorical STOP is compared with a separate binary-cross-entropy STOP head jointly trained with node classification (CMTP-BCE), repeated-node stopping, and a no-STOP control. Binary stop supervision alone is therefore not a new contribution for 2027.
topologicalplanning.results:
AUTHOR EXPERIMENT: Table 1, p 6: on unseen scenes with agent-generated maps, categorical stopping achieves 26.0% SR and separate BCE 27.3%; on R2R graphs the corresponding values are 28.7% and 30.2%. The no-STOP oracle success rates are 64.0% and 60.5% after 20 planning steps. That control adds exploration and does not isolate softmax normalization as the cause of stopping errors. Table 2, p 7 shows that heading hysteresis improves control: unseen agent-generated-map success rises 82.5→89.6 with variance 3. VERDICT: useful planner, controller and stopping ablations, with pre-exploration and sensor assumptions that prevent direct comparison to unknown-scene, single-run DUET.

Table 3/p 8 reports CMTP-BCE with R2R maps at 28.9 SR/24.1 SPL on unseen environments versus 26.4/22.7 for CMTP, but the autonomous-map setting has different values. Exploration distance is excluded from SPL; collected exploration is roughly 300 times the task navigation distance. Separate binary STOP prediction is therefore prior art, while its total deployment cost and map-availability assumptions differ from online DUET.

reverie.problem: REVERIE requires navigating to and identifying a remote object described by a high-level command, rather than merely stopping near a location. Object recognition and stopping are coupled: correct navigation alone is insufficient.
reverie.method: Section 3, PDF pp 4–5: 21,702 instructions refer to 4,140 target objects in 489 categories. Target boxes are projected from 3D object annotations into simulator views and retained within 3m. The agent receives panoramic RGB and navigable viewpoints and may output one target box or object ID. Selecting the correct supplied candidate, or predicting a box with IoU at least 0.5, counts as correct grounding. Multiple viewpoints may see the same object. The baseline combines FAST-short navigation with MAttNet subject, location and relation matching. For each view, the top three matching objects supply averaged visual features and BiLSTM-encoded category labels, concatenated with panorama features. Navigation uses action cross entropy and progress squared error. The pointer uses margin ranking: L=Σ[δ+S(o, r−)−S(o, r)]+ +[δ+S(o−, r)−S(o, r)]+, where positive object/expression pairs must outscore mismatched pairs by margin δ. Printed Eq 8 has a negative squared-error term and uses logit notation inside a logarithm; the released loss must disambiguate these rather than implementing the literal expression. Section 5.1 describes training the pointer first, then using its object information for navigator training, qualifying the compact joint-loss description.
reverie.novelty: A remote referring-expression benchmark and interactive navigator–pointer baseline couple navigation with object grounding. The task goes beyond goal proximity. However, supplied annotated object boxes are privileged perception proposals compared with detected boxes in a physical deployment.
reverie.results: AUTHOR EXPERIMENT: Table 3, p 8 reports test joint success 11.28% versus 7.07% for FAST plus a pointer and 77.84% for humans; navigation-only SR is 19.88%. Table 4 places the model at the true goal: MAttNet achieves 48.98% grounding accuracy versus 90.76% for humans, showing that object selection remains difficult even after navigation succeeds. The weak language-only baseline demonstrates a need for visual evidence, but does not prove every model uses every semantic relation. VERDICT: report RGS/RGSPL alongside SR/SPL, and distinguish ground-truth boxes from detected boxes. Goal-only datasets cannot replace this evaluation.

rxr.problem: RxR reduces R2R shortest-path and length biases and provides multilingual dense grounding. It contains 126,069 spoken and transcribed instructions in English, Hindi and Telugu over 16,522 paths, plus guide and follower pose traces. It directly tests whether agents follow route constraints instead of only reaching the goal.
rxr.method: Sections 3–4, PDF pp 3–6: sample a simple sequence of rooms, then find the shortest panorama path constrained to that sequence. Greedy selection favors coverage and paths that are not globally shortest. In total, 44.5% of paths are not globally shortest; the average is 14.9m and 27.4% longer than the shortest route. Spoken instruction timestamps are aligned through ASR/transcript dynamic time warping to six-degree-of-freedom poses. Human followers validate instructions and supply alternative paths. Primary metrics nDTW and sDTW measure path adherence because endpoint success alone is insufficient. The baseline in Section 5, p 7 uses multilingual BERT word features, a CNN text encoder, an LSTM policy and EfficientNet-B4 image features. Training mixes 50% behavioral cloning and 50% policy-gradient rollouts with incremental nDTW reward. The grounding auxiliary loss is L(z, m)=log Σi exp(zi)−log Σi mi exp(zi), equal to the negative log of attention mass on observed features, where binary mi labels regions viewed by the human. An analogous mask applies to words. Training uses 100k steps, batch 32 and Adam at 1e−4. Inference uses the full instruction and panorama; human traces supply supervision rather than test inputs.
rxr.novelty: Multilingual spoken instructions, dense pose alignment, varied paths that need not be shortest, and human alternative paths jointly strengthen the benchmark. The dataset offers supervision for language progress, but its own attention-supervision results are mixed. Annotation availability does not imply solved grounding.
rxr.results:
AUTHOR EXPERIMENT: Table 4, p 6: following the correct first step and then going straight achieves 27.2% SR on R2R versus 13.7% on RxR, supporting reduced shortcut bias. Table 5, p 8: combining guide and follower paths improves monolingual training; joint multilingual training and automatic translations can hurt. Visual attention supervision has mixed effects and textual attention masking did not improve performance. Table 6 shows weak direct transfer across datasets despite shared buildings. VERDICT: RxR is an essential control for route-faithfulness proposals. Report languages and guide/follower training conditions, and distinguish English subsets from the full multilingual benchmark.

Table 7, PDF p 9, trains/evaluates unimodal ablations rather than merely deleting a modality at test time: multimodal unseen SR 22.8 averages above the language-only and vision-only models; direction words can still guide actions using graph geometry without visual content. Appendix A/p 12 explains 247 annotators, separate Guide/Follower workers, pilot feedback and retraining below 80% success. The datasheet pp 19–21 confirms building-level splits inherited from MP3D/R2R and external simulator dependence. This collection protocol supports quality but does not establish immunity to all annotation or graph biases.
